text: Ahmed was kneeling in his garden with muddy gloves and a sore tooth. He could not decide whether to water the beans. He tapped his phone and said, 'Rain today?' The assistant checked the forecast and said no rain was coming until Thursday, and it would be sunny and warm until then. Ahmed wished to learn more, so he asked, 'Can you give me the weekly forecast for the garden?' The assistant read it out: sun on Monday and Tuesday, clouds on Wednesday, showers on Thursday, then dry again. Ahmed nodded and watered the beans. Then he asked for a reminder in the evening to cover the tomatoes if the wind picked up. The assistant said the reminder was set for seven o'clock. Ahmed pressed a hand to his cheek, smiled, and went back to the roses.

Tamar woke up late and squinted at her phone. 'Show me my new likes,' she mumbled. The assistant opened her notifications and said she had forty new likes and three comments. A huge crowd had come to see her photo from July at the lake. 'Reply to the first comment with a smiley,' she said. Then she changed her mind. 'No wait, not a smiley. Say thank you.' The assistant took away the smiley and posted 'Thank you!' under the comment. Tamar yawned and asked the assistant to mute her notifications until nine. It said they were muted until nine o'clock. She pulled the blanket back over her head.

Ayita woke up early and the whole house was quiet. Her brother had left a note on the kitchen table, but it was written in Spanish. 'Translate this,' she said, holding the phone over the paper. The assistant read the words and said the note meant: the dough is in the fridge, bake it at two hundred degrees for thirty minutes. Ayita opened the fridge. The dough had risen to the top of the bowl. 'Timer thirty minutes,' she said. The assistant started a thirty minute timer. She checked that the oven door was closed and turned the heat on. When the timer rang, the whole kitchen smelled like warm bread.

What should I pack for one night in a tent?
packing list for camping
what should i pack for a night in the hils
Make me a camping checklist
I'm going up into the hills tomorrow, what do I need to bring?
Camping list please
Can you list everything I need for sleeping outdoors for one night?
Could you please help me put together a list of what to take for a night in a tent?

Aiko was seven, and she wanted to go to her grandma's house. Mom was busy downstairs, so Aiko asked the tablet by herself. 'How long to Grandma's by bus?' she said. The assistant said the bus ride takes twenty minutes. 'And by car?' Aiko asked. The assistant said the car is faster and takes about half the time, ten minutes. Aiko ran downstairs. 'Mom, the tablet says the car takes half as long as the bus!' Mom laughed. 'Ask it where the nearest stop is.' Aiko asked, and the assistant said the bus stop was two streets away. 'Never mind, we'll take the car,' said Mom. Aiko cheered and grabbed her shoes.

- Help me plan food for my sister's birthday

- We're having people over, what do we eat?

people say:

- I never remember when the rubbish truck comes

- Do the glass bottles go out this week?

Ananya was packing lunches when she remembered her father's check-in. 'Call Dad tomorrow at nine,' she told the assistant. Then she stopped. 'No, make it ten. He sleeps later on Sundays.' The assistant changed the reminder to ten o'clock and said it would ring her phone and start the call. Ananya wished she could visit him more, but work kept her busy. 'Also remind him about his heart pills,' she said. The assistant said it would send her father a message at noon. He lived alone, and she worried constantly, so small things like this helped. She zipped the lunch bags, kissed her kids, and ran out the door.

A podcast app keeps your place. If you stop an episode halfway, it remembers where you left off, so you can pick it up later. People change a few things about it. Some want to go faster, so they say, 'Play at one and a half speed.' Others say, 'Skip back thirty seconds' when they miss a sentence, or 'Next chapter' in an audiobook. You can drag the bar with your finger, but many just ask out loud. Shows you like can sit in your library, like books on a store shelf. You might listen while cooking something crispy in the oven, hands busy, and say, 'Pause,' or 'Go back a bit,' and the app does it.

Person: Halve it.
Assistant: Sure. Which recipe should I halve?
Person: My family lasagna. I just got off a night shift and I only need to feed two.
Assistant: The lasagna is for eight. Do you want to reduce it to four servings?
Person: No, two.
Assistant: Then I'll cut it to a quarter. Most amounts are easy. The cheese goes from four cups to one cup, and the sauce from two cups to half a cup.
Person: Great, thanks. Read me the sauce part.
Assistant: Half a cup of tomato sauce, one spoon of oregano, and a pinch of salt.

When you order something online, the shop packs it and a driver brings it to your door. Sizes can be tricky. A shirt in medium might feel strange on you, and then you send it back for a refund or a different size. A heavy parcel, like a box of three umbrellas, may weigh a lot and take longer to arrive. People change their orders by saying, 'Make it a large,' 'Send it to my office instead,' or 'Cancel the second one.' If the box has not come, they ask, 'Where is my order?' and the shop tells them when it will arrive.

name: outfit_for_weather
does: Gives a short weather report for today, says what to wear, and tells you if it is a good time to open the windows.
inputs: your place, the day, and the first hour you will be outside
people say:
- What do I put on today?
- Do I need a coat?
- Is it warm enough for shorts?
- Will I get wet on my walk to work?
- How cold is it out there?
- Should I take a jacket for the kids?

First aid is what you do right away when someone gets a small injury, before a doctor can help. For a small burn, you hold the skin under cool running water for about ten minutes. A stream of cold water from the tap is best. For a small cut, you press a clean cloth on it until the bleeding stops. People often ask an assistant for help in the moment, and they say things like, 'My finger is burned, what do I do?' or 'Call an ambulance.' Keep your phone close and working. Stay with the person, and if the pain does not fade in half an hour, call a doctor.

Writing usually starts with a rough draft, and then you edit it. People ask for help with spelling, word counts and small changes. They say, 'How many words is this?', 'Fix the spelling in the last line' or 'Make this sound more cozy.' If a change goes wrong, they say, 'Undo.' Some writers pay for an app that checks their writing. If they do not like it, they can cancel and ask for a refund. Most of the time, though, writing is just a person, a page and a few good words.

Youssef had moved to the city only a month ago, and he did not know many people. His neighbor Sam had a birthday on Friday, and Youssef, who had a fever, did not want to forget it. 'Remind me to buy a card for Sam,' he said. Then he changed his mind. 'Actually, not a card. Give me a short list of gift ideas under twenty dollars.' The assistant said a small plant or a box of tea would be a good gift, and named two shops nearby. Youssef picked the tea. The assistant set a reminder for Thursday at five to pick it up. He thanked it, sipped some water, and went back to bed.

Stretch routine
Start my stretching
Give me ten minutes of easy stretches
My back is stiff, any stretches?
I want a gentle warm-up before my run
Walk me through a quick stretch session, please
Can you guide me through some stretches and keep track of how long I do them?
Cool down moves

Elif sat at her desk and stared at the calendar. Her friend's wedding was coming up, and she kept losing track of the days. 'How many days until June twentieth?' she asked her phone. The assistant said there were forty-two days. A shout came from down the hall, and Elif lost her train of thought. 'Sorry, I meant the twenty-seventh,' she said. The assistant counted again and said forty-nine days, which is exactly seven weeks. Elif sighed. She felt weak after a long morning, and the cups in the office sink were piling up, but at least the date was clear. 'Remind me one week before,' she said. The assistant set it.

Mikko grabbed his coat and ran toward the kitchen. He had a train to catch and a long article to read on the way. 'Excuse me, could you please make my coffee strong and not too sweet? I'm in a hurry, and I have a private call at nine, so I need to be awake for it,' he said to the coffee machine. The machine followed his words. It brewed a strong cup with only one spoon of sugar and said it would take two minutes. Mikko tapped his foot. When the light turned green, he poured the coffee into his travel cup, said thanks, and was out the door.

A washing machine cleans clothes with water and soap, and a dryer dries them with warm air. Most machines have programs: a short wash for a few clothes, a long one for dirty towels. People change the program by saying, 'Do a quick wash,' 'Make the water colder,' or 'Dry on low heat.' When the weather is rainy, many people use the dryer instead of a line outside. Before a trip, they pack clean clothes, so they ask, 'When will the load be done?' The assistant tells them how many minutes are left.

A video meeting lets people at different desks talk together. You join with a link or by saying, 'Join my ten o'clock call.' Before it starts, an agenda lists what everyone will talk about. People share their screen so others can see slides, and they often say, 'Share my screen,' 'Mute me,' or 'Turn off my camera.' Sit near a window or a lamp so your face has a soft glow, and keep your desk clean so the background looks tidy. If you work at a shared station in a busy office, you can ask for a quiet room before the call begins.

Tomas sat in his reading chair with a book, but the room felt too bright and harsh. The dryer was humming in the next room as it finished a load of towels. 'It's like a hospital in here,' he said to the smart speaker. The assistant understood that the lights were too strong. It lowered the ceiling light to thirty percent and changed the bulb to a warm color. Tomas smiled. 'A little less white, and maybe something blue by the window?' The assistant changed the lamp by the window to a soft blue. 'Perfect,' said Tomas, and he turned the page.

Kofi was feeding his baby when he spotted a bill on the table. The shiny new bank card had come in the mail, but he needed to move some money first. 'How much is in my savings?' he asked. The assistant said there was four hundred dollars in savings and nine hundred in checking. 'Move half of my savings to checking,' he said. The assistant moved two hundred dollars from savings to checking and said the new balance in checking was eleven hundred. Kofi nodded. He also asked it to remind him to pay the cable bill on Friday. The assistant set the reminder. Kofi wiped the baby's chin and went back to feeding.

Clocks show what time it is where you are, but the world has many time zones. When it is noon in London, it is seven in the morning in New York. People who call family far away often check the time first, because nobody wants to wake a friend at night. They say, 'What time is it in Tokyo?' or 'Is it too late to call Sam in Sydney?' Some people hate doing the math in their head, and they are lucky to have a watch or phone that does it for them. When they travel, they can also say, 'Change my clock to local time.'

A text message is a short note you send to someone's phone. People write one to a friend, or to a group chat with many people. When you cannot type, you can say, 'Text Mia I am running late,' and your phone writes and sends it. You can also ask, 'Read my new messages' or 'Reply sorry, I can't come.' A delivery driver who earns tips by the hour cannot hold a phone, so they talk to it. If you will be late to the theater, a quick text saves a lot of worry. And before it goes out, you can say, 'Change it to nine thirty.'

Tessa woke up to a strange noise outside. It sounded like a dog crying. The house was cold, and she did not want to go out in her slippers. 'Brr, my feet are ice,' she said to the speaker. The assistant understood and turned the heat up to twenty-one degrees. Then Tessa asked, 'Has anyone posted about a missing dog?' The assistant checked the neighborhood board and said a neighbor had posted that a brown dog named Ocean had been missing since last night. Tessa put on her coat and boots, grabbed a leash, and went out to look for him.

Kwame sat in the corner of the library with a history essay due on Friday. His shirt for tomorrow's presentation needed an iron too, but that could wait. 'Don't set a reminder for tonight,' he told his phone. 'I don't want to be bothered until after dinner.' The assistant said okay, no reminders tonight. 'Instead, remind me tomorrow at seven to iron my shirt.' The assistant set it. Kwame opened a sweet snack, a peanut butter bar, and went back to the essay. Then he asked, 'How many days until the essay is due?' The assistant said three days.

A smart lock lets you open or close your front door without a key. It is for safety, and for letting people in when you are not home. People who travel often feel nervous about leaving the door open, so they ask, 'Did I lock the door?' or 'Lock up the house.' You can also say, 'Let my neighbor in at three' or 'Who is at the door?' A camera by the door shows the path, the tree by the gate and any visitor or delivery person. When the garage door is open, you can say, 'Close the garage.'

A morning drink is a small ritual. Coffee, tea and smoothies can be made stronger, weaker or sweeter, and people tell the machine or the assistant what they like. They say, 'Make it stronger,' 'Less sugar,' 'A little more milk' or 'Hot, not warm.' Someone who feels hungry may ask for a smoothie with banana and oats. If you are stuck in traffic and worry about being late, you might ask for a quick tea at the next stop. It is the little changes, a bit more here and a bit less there, that make a drink yours.

When you order food for delivery, a restaurant cooks the meal and a driver brings it to you. The app shows how long it will take. Hungry people often ask, 'Where is my order?' or 'How long now?' You can change things too: 'No onions,' 'Make it two burgers,' or 'Leave it at the door.' A tip is a thank you to the driver, and many people say, 'Tip ten percent.' When the food comes, you unpack the bag and check it. Some people write a personal note like, 'Ring twice, the baby sleeps.' The app may also send news about delays.

Nathan sat in his office chair and needed quiet music to focus. He had an urgent report to finish. 'Play something calm,' he said to his phone. The assistant started a playlist of soft piano. Just then he had to sneeze, and the music seemed too loud. 'A little lower,' he said, and the volume went down. 'And at quarter to ten, pause the music, please. I have a call.' The assistant said it would pause the music at quarter to ten. Nathan nodded, typed the last page of the report, and reached for a tissue.

Wiremu was fixing a fan when the house got hotter. He had a screw in one hand and a toddler on his lap. 'Turn on the air conditioning, but not in the baby's room,' he said. The assistant turned on the cooling in the living room and left the nursery alone. The thermostat was offline for a moment, so the assistant waited and then set it to twenty-three degrees. 'Don't make it too cold,' Wiremu added. He swiped on his phone to check the temperature. It showed twenty-six, and falling. He put down the screw and relaxed.

Sofia had moved to a new city, and she did not know the buses yet. Her sister would call at six, and Sofia expected a serious talk about money. 'Could you please remind me at half past five to leave work? I'm still learning the buses, and I don't want to be late for my sister's call,' she said. The assistant set a reminder for half past five and said it would ring twice. 'Also, remind me when I get near the corner shop to buy milk.' The assistant said it would remind her when she was nearby. Sofia smiled, shut her laptop and started to pack her bag.

Many older people live alone, and their families like to know they are safe. A check-in call is a short chat each day. If the person does not answer, the family gets a message. Medicine reminders say when to take a pill. If something goes wrong, like a fall, the person can say, 'Call for help,' and the phone calls a nearby neighbor or an ambulance. People also say, 'Call my daughter' or 'Remind me about my pills at eight.' They try not to break their routine, and an invitation to tea at a neighbor's house can be a good reminder too.

Assistant: The website is open, and your reminder is set for 6:30.

A robot vacuum drives around the floor and picks up dust by itself. It is for people who don't have time to sweep. You can change how it works: 'Clean the kitchen only,' 'Clean at ten every morning,' or 'Use medium suction.' Some robots can't climb over a thing above a certain height, like a thick rug. Before guests come, many people invite the robot to run: 'Vacuum before my friends arrive.' When it is done, it goes back to its charger. 'Stop cleaning' or 'Go home' calls it back.

Walter was texting his friends while he sat in class. Ten people wanted to meet at the park on Saturday, but his calendar looked full. 'How many things do I have on Saturday?' he asked. The assistant said he had three: soccer at nine, a haircut at noon, and dinner with his aunt. Everything blue on his calendar was school stuff, and there was none on Saturday. 'Move the haircut to Sunday,' he said. The assistant moved it. He wanted to decrease the time soccer took, so he said, 'Make soccer half an hour shorter.' The assistant changed it to end at nine thirty. Walter texted his friends: see you at the park at ten.

Zana was a retired teacher, and her dad was coming to visit that afternoon. 'Could you please start the robot vacuum in the living room and the hall now? My dad is coming at three, and dust makes him cough,' she said politely. The assistant started the robot and said it would finish in about forty minutes. It was hot in the house, so Zana asked the assistant to turn on the fan. It did. Then she said, 'Turn off the vacuum at two thirty, please.' The assistant set that. Zana poured a cold glass of water and waited for the sound of the robot to stop.

Diego was in the kitchen cooking a big dinner, and his cousin was waiting on a video call from Lisbon. He poured a little wine into the sauce and stirred. 'I hope it's not too late for my cousin,' he said to his speaker. The assistant understood and said it was ten at night local time in Lisbon, and five in the afternoon where Diego was. 'A bit late, but still okay for a call,' it said. Diego smiled, turned the heat down under the pot, and pressed the call button. His cousin's face came up on the screen, already in pajamas.

Pooja finished her homework and sat on the sofa. 'There's nothing to watch and I'm so bored,' she said to her phone. The assistant understood that she wanted a film, and it listed three movies at the cinema nearby tonight, including a travel adventure. She picked the adventure. 'Is there a show after six?' she asked. The assistant said there was one at seven thirty. Pooja looked at her shoes, which were dirty from the park. 'I'd better change,' she said. She asked the assistant to remind her to buy candy at the shop on the way, and it did.

people say:

- Start tracking my run
- How far did I go this morning?
- Am I faster than yesterday?
- Tell my friends I did five kilometers
- Did I reach my goal?

A reminder is a small note that rings at a time or place so you do not forget. People use them for pills, birthdays, or taking out the rubbish. You can say, 'Remind me at five to call Mom,' or 'Remind me when I get home to water the plants.' The sound is sharp so you notice it. If a reminder comes at the wrong time, say 'Snooze ten minutes' or 'Change it to six.' To start fresh, you can reset it or clear all of them. A note on the sink that says wash the cups is a reminder too.
